cases.question: What is known about SGLT2 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes, kidney disease, and heart failure?
cases.answer: SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, hospitalization for heart failure or cardiovascular death, and all-cause mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes [S1]. These benefits are consistent regardless of whether patients are receiving metformin [S1]. Additionally, SGLT2 inhibitors improve kidney outcomes, including reducing the risk of chronic kidney disease progression [S1].

cases.answer: Yes, the retrieved evidence describes that SGLT2 inhibitors reduced major adverse cardiovascular events, hospitalization for heart failure or cardiovascular death, and all-cause mortality consistently, whether patients were receiving metformin or not [S1].

cases.question: What were the benefits and harms of intensive systolic blood pressure control in SPRINT?
cases.answer: Intensive systolic blood pressure control below 120 mm Hg compared to standard control below 140 mm Hg reduced major cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality [S1]. However, it also increased the frequency of serious adverse events such as hypotension, syncope, electrolyte abnormalities, and acute kidney injury or failure [S1].

cases.question: Did the SPRINT blood pressure trial include patients with diabetes?
cases.answer: No, the SPRINT randomized clinical trial excluded patients with diabetes and prior stroke [S2].

cases.question: How do inhaled corticosteroids help prevent asthma exacerbations?
cases.answer: Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are effective for preventing asthma exacerbations by reducing airway inflammation and improving lung function [S1]. Strategies include daily controller treatment, intermittent high-dose ICS in selected patients, and as-needed dosing with a rescue inhaler for mild asthma [S1].

cases.question: What inhaled corticosteroid strategies are discussed for mild asthma?

cases.question: How do DOACs compare with warfarin for bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation?
cases.answer: Bleeding risk comparisons between direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) and warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation patients show variability [S1]. Apixaban has been associated with a lower bleeding risk compared to warfarin, whereas rivaroxaban did not demonstrate the same reduction [S1].

cases.question: What medications are used for peripheral artery disease?
cases.answer: For symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD), single antiplatelet therapy is recommended to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events [S1]. Aspirin or clopidogrel can be used for this purpose [S1].

final_documents.title: 2024 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline for Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease: Key Points

cases.question: When is low-dose rivaroxaban plus aspirin used in PAD?
cases.answer: Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily combined with low-dose aspirin is recommended to reduce major adverse cardiovascular and limb events in symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) after endovascular or surgical revascularization [S1].

final_documents.title: 2024 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline for Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease: Key Points

cases.question: Should full-intensity oral anticoagulation be used only to reduce PAD cardiovascular or limb events?
cases.answer: Full-intensity oral anticoagulation should not be used solely to reduce peripheral artery disease (PAD) cardiovascular or limb events when there is no other indication such as atrial fibrillation [S1].
